author: Rachel Aroesti
description:
Refugee Peter Sichel was known as ‘the Jewish James Bond’ after fleeing Germany and becoming an integral cold war-era spy. He died last year but, at 100-years-old, he told his remarkable story for this film

Why, exactly, was Peter Sichel “the last spy”? It’s not something Katharina Otto-Bernstein’s documentary about the cold war-era CIA man clarifies. The “Jewish James Bond” – as a woman from his synagogue nicknames him – is a catchier moniker, although that’s not quite right either. If Sichel was once a swashbuckling secret agent, we don’t hear much about his escapades here. Instead, he seems closer to M: sitting behind a desk pulling strings while his agents risked life and limb sneaking around the German Democratic Republic.

The Last Spy begins as a straightforward but riveting biography built around a long, candid interview with Sichel, who was 100 at the time of filming (he died last year at 102). We hear about his childhood in Germany, which was initially privile
title: The Last Spy review – a riveting tale of CIA meddling, espionage gossip and Blue Nun wine

author: Guardian sport and agencies
description:
• Haaland’s late penalty grabs Norway last-eight spot

  • Parrott penalties help Republic of Ireland secure playoff

A wonder strike from Justin Devenny earned Northern Ireland top spot in Nations League Group B2 and promotion to the top tier of the competition. The Stoke player fired home on the volley from the edge of the area to earn a 1-1 draw away to Hungary, who would have leapfrogged Michael O’Neill’s side in the group with victory.

Northern Ireland had fallen 1-0 behind after a 35th-minute goal from the striker Barnabás Varga, who slotted home when one-on-one with the goalkeeper Pierce Charles after a defensive mix-up. The goal ended Northern Ireland’s proud record of not having conceded in this campaign and also sent Hungary to the top of the group in the live standings.

Continue readin
title: Nations League roundup: Devenny’s divine strike lifts Northern Ireland to top tier

author: Miatta Mbriwa and Anandita Abraham
description:
Students oppose appearance of self-described ‘race realist’ who made plagiarism claims against Jason Arday

Hundreds of protesters filled the cobbled streets around Oriel College, Oxford, to voice their opposition to an appearance by Nathan Cofnas, the self-described “race realist”.

The event organised by the university’s Reform UK student society – billed as “An evening with Nathan Cofnas: is DEI undermining higher education?” – went ahead on Tuesday evening despite opposition from students, college staff and local politicians concerned that his appearance would create a hostile environment.

Continue reading...
title: Hundreds protest against Nathan Cofnas talk on DEI at Oriel College in Oxford

author: Ben Fisher at Cardiff City Stadium
description:
One way or another, Portugal’s No 7 shirt has caused quite the commotion in recent weeks and months, if not years. Perhaps it was inevitable, then, that the first win of the post-Cristiano Ronaldo era would come courtesy of the player wearing the updated jersey, one with a cross through the number to preserve Ronaldo’s eternal legacy, as the Portuguese football federation put it. A sumptuous finish by Carlos Forbs, a second-half substitute, was ultimately enough to clinch victory on a topsy-turvy night with Portugal surviving Pedro Neto’s sending-off for two yellow cards.

Turn a new page and all that. This was a welcome victory for Jorge Jesus, for whom a 4-1 home defeat to Denmark a few days ago was a harrowing juncture, and there were plenty of positive takeaways for Wales, too. David Brooks cancelled out Bruno Fernandes’s opener from the edge of the box and then seized the lead through Sorba Thomas, who applied the finishing touch to a purring team move. But Neto, who pick
title: Portugal’s new No 7 Forbs channels Ronaldo for winner as Wales are denied

author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
description:
President, who had agreed to sit for deposition in October but backed out, must now appear by 22 January

Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge,gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned.

Continue reading...
title: Judge extends deadline for Trump’s deposition in $10bn BBC lawsuit

author: Agence France-Presse
description:
Indigenous Awá people of Amazon make contact with villagers and accept food to take back to territory

About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.

According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.

Continue reading...
title: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life

author: Alex Burgis
description:
0My father, Pete Burgis, who has died aged 65, was an internationally acclaimed Foley artist whose work brought physical reality to films and television dramas.

Foley – named after the pioneerng Warner Brothers sound engineer Jack Foley – is the art of creating sounds in sync with the picture, from footsteps and rustling clothes to the movements of creatures. Pete understood that these were not simply technical details but performances that could convey character, emotion and story. He won two Emmy awards, for Band of Brothers, in 2002, and Generation Kill, in 2009.

Continue reading...
title: Pete Burgis obituary

author: Robert Kitson
description:
Springboks’ achievements are remarkable but their head coach lacks statesmanship, diplomacy and good grace in defeat

So here we go again. Exactly five years have passed since South Africa’s head coach, Rassie Erasmus, first felt the full force of World Rugby’s ire for criticising match officials. And guess what? This most habitual of offenders has just copped another lengthy ban – and deservedly so – for his latest intemperate comments, notable as ever for their total lack of statesmanship, diplomacy or good grace in defeat.

To his acolytes his outspoken nature is part of what makes Rassie such a groot leier (great leader). To many others it simply cements his status as a serial prat. For the avoidance of
title: Rassie Erasmus’s tired ref-blaming act is wearing thin – South Africa deserve better | Robert Kitson

author: Sally Weale Education correspondent
description:
Vice-chancellor halts proposed relocation from Stratford-upon-Avon but offers no guarantees over future

The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move its much-loved Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to its city campus after an outcry from scholars, actors and enthusiasts around the world.

Prof Adam Tickell, the university’s vice-chancellor and principal, issued a statement on Tuesday evening saying proposals to relocate the institute and its renowned 60,000-volume library to the university’s Edgbaston campus would be put on hold while its future was explored.

Continue reading...
title: University of Birmingham pauses plans to move Shakespeare Institute after outcry

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested by British police on 10 November over allegations related to espionage

A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said.

Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, 41, was detained by British counter-terrorism police ‌on 10 November in Gloucestershire over allegations relating ⁠to espionage.

Continue reading...
title: American soldier held in UK suspected of spying for Russia taken into US military custody

author: Lorenzo Tondo and Sufian Taha in Jerusalem
description:
Bullet hit 72-year-old Fadha Wadha in head outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, in the West Bank, say residents

A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in a village near Jericho where settlers have recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta in the occupied West Bank when she was struck in the head by a bullet as Israeli settlers fired towards Palestinian houses, according to testimonies from residents. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were wounded by gunfire.

Continue reading...
title: Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say

author: Paul MacInnes
description:
At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’

After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 43-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.”

In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4m) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the English players’ union observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money.
title: ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future

author: Haroon Siddique Legal affairs correspondent
description:
Woman sued by alleged rapist tells justice committee that Slapp lawsuits present perpetrator as victim of wrongdoing

Attempts by perpetrators and alleged perpetrators of sexual abuse to silence their victims using the law are “the ultimate form of gaslighting”, MPs have heard.

Verity Nevitt, a co-founder of the Gemini Project, a survivor-led nonprofit organisation, told the House of Commons justice committee about the ordeal of being sued by the man she and her sister, Lucy, respectively accused of sexual abuse and rape.

Continue reading...
title: Using law to try to silence abuse victims is ‘ultimate form of gaslighting’, MPs told

author: Kiran Stacey and Richard Partington
description:
Youth unemployment review risks clash with unions and Labour left over workers’ rights and minimum wage

  • Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s youth unemployment report?

  • Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

  • Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people

Alan Milburn has called on ministers to cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people, setting up a potential clash with trade unions and the Labour left over employment rights.

The former health secreta
title: Milburn calls for tax cuts for businesses hiring young people despite union concerns

author: Editorial
description:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has
title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial

author: Editorial
description:
Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has
title: The Guardian view on climate debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial

author: John Crace
description:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sur
title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision

author: Damien Gayle, Fiona Harvey, Graham Readfearn and Gabrielle Canon in Antalya
description:
Britain joins other signatories to statement urging introduction of targeted taxes on heavy emitters

The UK has signed a statement that backs levies on polluting sectors to pay for the impacts of the climate crisis, in a strong political signal that could pave the way for frequent flyer and crypto taxes.

Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

Continue readin
title: UK backs idea of new levies on polluting sectors to pay for climate action costs

author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Catherine Shoard ; produced by Angus Neale ; senior producer Leonore Schick ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
description:
It’s official: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond. The British actor is known for leading roles in the Hollywood franchises Twilight, The Batman and Dune. Pattinson entered the race for Bond at a relatively late stage, beating earlier frontrunners including Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor. With 007’s identity confirmed, what will the new Bond era look like? Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s film editor, Catherine Shoard

Continue reading...
title: Is Robert Pattinson the right choice for James Bond? - The Latest

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers recount their terrifying experiences of sleep paralysis in response to an article by Amy Fleming

I experienced sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations from childhood and into adulthood, with the episodes only waning in my 30s (Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis, 11 November). I never spoke about them to anyone.

I experienced hallucinations in the form of severe perspective distortion (oversized bed and rooms) and full hallucinations/dream states, auditory hallucinations (screaming and loud thumping) and, of course, paralysis. I didn’t know at what point I was asleep or if I had woken and could easily slip back into a hypnagogic state. I only became aware of this state as an adult, having been referred to a psychiatrist on an unrelated matter.
title: Sleep paralysis: when you’re awake, but can’t move – or even breathe | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Tara Padfield will be buying her marmalade and leaving the trees in the woods; Jen Arnall-Culliford says cooking in advance is key. Plus a letter from Alan Ravenscroft

I read Ammar Kalia’s article (Christmas is all in the preparation! Chefs on eight easy things to do now – so you can relax on the big day, 12 November) with a mixture of disbelief and mounting despair.

Apparently, the secret to a stress-free Christmas involves roasting a kilogram of chicken wings and simmering stock for hours, making marmalade from scratch, infusing gin with Sichuan peppercorns and, should we have a spare afternoon, heading into the woods to forage for Douglas fir needles. I had naively imagined that time-saving tips might actually save time.
title: Have yourself a stress-free Christmas | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to a letter suggesting that location scouts for a new site look beyond Manchester, Liverpool and Birmingham

Maggie Hamilton is right (Letters, 12 November): parliament should move to the north-east of England. The city of the Prince Bishops, Durham, would be an ideal choice.

We already have a ready-made and renovated “pitman’s parliament” debating chamber and offices in the historic Redhills building of the Durham Miners’ Association. This is only a five-minute walk from the railway station, which has hourly trains to all points south, including nearby Darlington with its “Treasury North” office, so very convenient. Just around the corner is a brand new, massive and unoccupied riverside office block, apartment and hotel complex. Ideal for business and overnight stays when in session.
title: Durham city would be a canny place for parliament | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Grow kits | Cat’s humans | Stink bombs | Fascinating facts | Crossword clues

Re your report (Mushroom lovers in UK told to avoid grow kits owing to invasive species risk, 16 November), anyone contemplating mushroom grow kits should read Ray Bradbury’s 1962 short story Boys! Raise Giant Mushrooms in Your Cellar! If it doesn’t send you screaming out of the house, it’ll certainly put you off growing, or eating, mushrooms.
Lynne Scrimshaw
London

• It is possible to own a dog, but not to be “a cat owner” (Pass notes, 16 November); a cat will simply move somewhere else if it chooses. Putting its food in an inaccessible transparent box will certainly accelerate it relocating to where th
title: Ray Bradbury’s warning against mushroom-growing | Brief letters

author: Pippa Crerar political editor
description:
PM to wait until after Brussels summit at which he hopes for agreements on food, farming and emissions

  • UK politics live – latest updates

Andy Burnham has said there is “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer term relationship with the EU, as he comes under pressure from his own party to press the brakes on the pace of the rethink.

The prime minister said he would “take stock” of the wider relationship after Friday’s summit in Brussels at which he hopes to secure agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

Continue reading...
title: Andy Burnham delays taking stock  of UK’s relationship with EU

author: William Christou
description:
Digital monitors recorded 400% rise in posts attacking Arab Israelis, including Netanyahu’s disproven fraud allegations

Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media in Israel around the country’s general election last month, digital monitors have said, as politicians including Benjamin Netanyahu levelled disproven allegations against Arab Israeli parties of election fraud.

A new report by the Israel-based Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter recorded a deluge of anti-Arab discourse across social media platforms such as X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in the days surrounding Israel’s 27 October election.

Continue reading...
title: Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media during Israel’s election, report finds

author: Luke Harding in Kyiv
description:
With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea

At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.

Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated w
title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule

description:
On a visit to Preston, the royal revealed his favourite classic filling. But with jacket potatoes as far as the eye could see, he surprisingly failed to order one ...

Name: Jacket potatoes.

Age: As everyone knows, potatoes originated in South America where Incas cooked them in a huatia, an oven dug in the earth. So quite ancient.

title: Spud-one-likes: is King Charles really a baked potato aficionado?

author: Raphaël Jucobin in Paris
description:
• French FA chief officially begins bid for Fifa presidency

  • Uefa’s choice hints at ‘support from other continents’

Philippe Diallo, Europe’s candidate to fight Gianni Infantino for the Fifa presidency, said he had received “strong signs of support from other continents” as he launched his campaign in Paris on Tuesday.

The French Football Federation president also said he had contacted Kozo Tashima, who announced his candidacy this month, and would try to convince him to “join forces”. Diallo did not indicate whether he would explicitly be asking Tashima to stand aside. “Our approaches are based on the same assessments and the same values,” he said.

Continue reading...
title: ‘I’m entering to win’: Philippe Diallo launches campaign to topple Gianni Infantino

author: Blake Montgomery and Johana Bhuiyan
description:
Huang makes first statement since resigning, while board of directors is not considering reinstating him, reports say

Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company Thursday.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen i
title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia as CEO

author: Dan Sabbagh Kyiv
description:
Partial demolition of bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea is obvious embarrassment to Putin days before meeting with Xi and Trump

  • Europe live – latest updates

Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long range drones.

The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing, one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir
title: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play

author: Jonathan Watts
description:
We look at what is happening over the Arctic and what it might mean for winter weather in the northern hemisphere

The polar vortex has flipped direction, signalling the earliest “major sudden stratospheric warming” ever observed. We examine how it is likely to affect you and whether it will bring snow.

Continue reading...
title: What is the polar vortex, why has it flipped and will it bring the UK snow?

author: Kate Connolly in Berlin
description:
Pop-singing sisters, who died together aged 89 last year, described declining health and expressed gratitude assisted dying was an option

Alice and Ellen Kessler, the identical pop-singing twins who chose to jointly end their lives through assisted dying last year, said they had “reached rock bottom” due to health problems and had been relieved to be able to die together.

The sisters, who became huge television stars in the 1960s and 70s, especially in Italy and the US, said a catalogue of health conditions had left them with no desire to carry on living.

Continue reading...
title: ‘We will have been spared a lot’: Kessler twins explained assisted dying decision in final letter

description:
